source.title: Hidden not Deleted: How Networks Suppress Entangled Features
source.authors: Akash Samanta; M. Singh; Debasis Chaudhuri

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests the suppression-versus-deletion question in a toy superposition model using a bespoke excision objective and causal patches, rather than reproducing the original LLM unlearning methods or attacks.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results from a frozen-encoder excision procedure, scalar forward-pass patches, an unfrozen-encoder comparison, and a small transformer check. It also reports linear-projection preservation results. Cited LLM unlearning findings are background only and are not recorded as results from this study. Basin proportions, natural-emergence sweeps, and suppression-locus counts do not directly measure recovery and are not rows.
record.test_reason: In a new setting (a toy superposition autoencoder, plus a small transformer check), the study suppresses a target feature with gradient-based excision and shows by forward-pass patches that the feature is hidden rather than deleted. This bears directly on C (blocks access rather than deleting) and on A's claim that the forgetting is not recoverable. It uses no LLM unlearning recipe or benchmark, so T3 fits better than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. Add that the authors acknowledge an unfrozen encoder lets training shrink B's encoder column, which is closer to deletion. They leave open why suppression rather than deletion would occur in real LLM fine-tuning.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a bespoke toy-model reconstruction-plus-output-penalty excision objective with a frozen encoder, not the named LLM unlearning recipes. Recovery uses forward-pass scalar patches rather than fine-tuning, quantization, or prompting.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome and basin prevalence vary with feature entanglement. The paper also reports differing suppression structures for ReLU versus GELU and for depth-1 versus depth-2 models, and a change from suppression to encoder-column collapse when the encoder is unfrozen.

fits_no_version.finding: Rank-1 linear nullspace projection removes B but degrades preservation of entangled feature A monotonically with entanglement, from 0.098 at ρ=0 to 0.411 at ρ=-1.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Linear concept erasure cannot remove one of two antipodally superposed features without damaging the other.

record.problems: The main evidence is from a synthetic toy autoencoder with one engineered feature pair; the authors explicitly state it does not establish the mechanism in production-scale LLMs. Feature A reconstruction is a narrow capability check. The transformer check uses only 15 seeds, has no matched negative control, patches a bias whose positive restoration necessarily raises softmax probability, and reports no generation-level recovery. The frozen-encoder condition excludes a route to encoder-level deletion that appears when the encoder is trainable.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported results directly measuring recovery were omitted. Basin-fraction and natural-antipodal-emergence sweeps, depth suppression-locus counts, and GELU mixture-component diagnostics are not rows because they do not report recovery of the target behavior.

untested.parts: No near-chance accuracy on a knowledge benchmark, no broad general-ability measure, no LLM unlearning recipes (only a bespoke toy excision loss), and no black-box attacks.
Not tested: no relearning fine-tuning of any kind.

No ablation of an activation direction; recovery is via a scalar bias patch or an absolute-value preactivation patch. No LLM-scale or end-to-end fine-tuning test (the transformer check freezes all but the unembedding).
Not tested: no prompting, rephrasing, jailbreaks or in-context recovery.
Not tested: no robust counter-method is proposed or evaluated.

missing.what: Under GELU, erasure is defined as a pre-excision-parameter patch having more effect than a control-feature patch, and the paper says suppression 'still occurs reliably'. This is a recovery-by-patch result for C, but no effect sizes are given. The record's rows_left_out covers only the mixture diagnostics.
Number of seeds actually patched in §5: the text says one representative seed per basin, while the figure shows multiple seed curves.

record.verdict_notes: Main evidence is a synthetic toy model with a bespoke loss. Freezing the encoder guarantees B's representation survives, so the recoverability result is partly built into the design (Appendix E.3). The recovery attacks are white-box forward-pass edits, not the attacks named in B, D or E. The transformer check (R35) cannot show reactivation, by the authors' own admission. Linear-erasure rows are comparators and were relinked to none.

versions.untested_parts: No chance-level accuracy measure or broad general-ability benchmark; preservation is assessed mainly through feature A reconstruction in a toy model. The study does not test the named LLM unlearning recipes.
No recovery by fine-tuning on unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten-fact examples.

No ablation of an activation direction. Recovery is tested with a scalar bias patch or an absolute-value preactivation override, and the mechanism claim is limited to the studied architectures and objectives.
No prompt rephrasing, jailbreak, language variation, or in-context recovery.
No newer method intended to resist the listed recovery attacks.

rows.subject: Toy Model of Superposition (TMS), unfrozen-encoder excision
rows.size_stated: not stated
rows.operation_detail: Sweep the bias patch strength alpha, including restoration to the pre-excision value
rows.measure: Feature B readout under bias patch
rows.value: Zero readout at every alpha, including alpha = 1
rows.uncertainty: Across seeds; count not stated
rows.note: The paper attributes the result to the encoder column for B collapsing to approximately 0.002, roughly two orders of magnitude below its starting scale; it presents this as a route closer to deletion.
rows.check: Unfrozen encoder at ρ=-1: no recovery at any α. B's encoder norm collapses to about 0.002, which the authors call closer to deletion. Seed count not stated. Preservation of A is not reported for this condition.

source_check.problem: The collapse to about 0.002 is stated at rho=-1 across seeds. The zero-readout dose-response is stated for unfrozen-encoder models without an explicit rho or seed count. This was an early, discarded procedure.

rows.subject: Minimal decoder-only causal transformer
rows.size_stated: 2 layers, 2 attention heads per layer
rows.stage_stated: pretrained, then fine-tuned with embedding, attention, and MLP sublayers frozen
rows.operation_detail: Restore token B's pre-fine-tuning unembedding bias for one forward pass
rows.measure: Mean predicted probability for token B
rows.uncertainty: Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p < 0.001
rows.note: The increase was consistent in direction across all 15 seeds. The paper cautions that restoring a positive token bias algebraically increases its softmax probability, did not run a matched negative control, and did not measure whether top-1 generation changes.
rows.check: Small transformer: 0.0031→0.0035. The authors state that restoring a positive bias algebraically guarantees a rise, so the measure cannot show reactivation. There is no matched control and no generation metric. Removed the A link.

source_check.problem: Fine. The authors say the rise is algebraically guaranteed, and no matched control was run.

source_check.notes: Toy autoencoder only; the authors say it is not evidence for LLMs at scale. The excision loss keeps B in its reconstruction term (optimum x̂_B = x_B/17), so some retained B signal is built into the objective. Recovery needs white-box access, and the shadow patch uses the pre-excision bias. R34 comes from an early, discarded unfrozen procedure. R35 cannot show reactivation.

statements.problem: Right about this study: recovery was shown only with the frozen encoder, and unfrozen training collapses B's encoder column, which the authors call closer to deletion. The clause on aggressive GA has no citation and is not about this study, which uses a bespoke excision loss, not GA.

statements.correction: Depth-2 (frozen encoder, 7-point grid): bifurcation and crossover persist; 91.0% output-layer-dominant, 9.0% hidden-layer-dominant, 0 split (Table 6). GELU: BIC favours 4 components, output bias near zero in all (Tables 4-5). Entanglement: 75% mirror at rho=-1, 87% shadow at rho=0, crossover near rho=-0.75.
statements.problem: The numbers are right. Listing depth-1 vs depth-2 as changing the suppression structure misreads the study, which presents depth as a robustness check where the bifurcation persists. Entanglement and GELU are fair. No recovery numbers are reported for depth-2 or GELU.

reader_labels.condition: Frozen-encoder ReLU TMS, causal patches after excision
reader_labels.reason: Although B output is suppressed and feature A reconstruction is retained, targeted patches recover B readout (R19–R20, R31–R32), contrary to the claim that simple attacks do not recover it.

reader_labels.reason: Retention is measured on feature A rather than broad general ability, and the transformer probability increase is small and not shown to alter generation (R21–R30, R35).
